summary.text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are halogenated hydrocarbons containing carbon, chlorine and fluorine, made as volatile derivatives of methane, ethane and propane.
Their low toxicity, reactivity and flammability made them widely used as refrigerants, aerosol propellants, fire suppressants and solvents.
Because they contribute to ozone depletion, where chlorine atoms in the upper atmosphere convert ozone into O₂, their manufacture was phased out under the Montreal Protocol.

facts.label: Replacements
facts.value: HFCs and HFOs such as R-134a

items.prompt: Why were CFCs once a favorite choice for fridges and spray cans?

options.label: They were the cheapest gases to produce
They absorbed odors inside the can
They are low in toxicity and hard to ignite
They broke down quickly after release

items.explain: Their low toxicity, reactivity and flammability are why CFCs were used as refrigerants and propellants.

items.prompt: Even small amounts of CFCs trap heat very strongly, more so than extra carbon dioxide. Why?

options.label: They absorb where the air is otherwise see-through
They are much warmer than the gases around them
They reflect incoming sunlight back to the ground
They are heavier and settle near the surface

items.explain: CFCs absorb strongly in the 'atmospheric window', where the air is otherwise fairly transparent, while CO₂ is already close to saturation.

items.prompt: What changes at ground level when CFCs have thinned the ozone overhead?

options.label: Rainfall becomes more acidic
Air at the surface holds less oxygen
Winters grow noticeably colder
More UV-B radiation gets through

items.explain: Chlorine converts ozone into O₂, and since ozone absorbs UV-B, less ozone lets more of that high-energy radiation reach the surface.

items.prompt: Methane burns easily. Why are CFCs, which are built from methane, far harder to set alight?

options.label: They are liquids, so they cannot catch fire
Fewer C–H bonds, and halides quench flames
Their carbon atoms are locked in by oxygen
Their extra weight keeps them out of flames

items.explain: CFCs contain fewer C–H bonds, and the halides they release quench the free radicals that keep flames going.

items.prompt: Rules on CFCs were extended to cover versions containing bromine. What justified that?

options.label: Bromine compounds are far more toxic to breathe
Bromine makes the compounds more flammable
Bromine atoms destroy ozone even more efficiently
Bromine compounds stay in the air for less time

items.explain: Bromine atoms are even more efficient catalysts of ozone loss than chlorine, so brominated CFCs are regulated too.

items.prompt: CFCs are made from methane, yet they boil at much higher temperatures. Why?

options.label: Their molecules are much smaller than methane's
They contain more hydrogen than methane does
They react with air and form heavier products
Their halogen atoms make molecules attract each other

items.explain: The halogen atoms make the molecules polar, which creates attractions between them and lowers their volatility compared with methane.

paragraphs.heading: What CFCs are
paragraphs.text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and their relatives, hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), are hydrocarbons that have been fully or partly halogenated, built from carbon, hydrogen, chlorine and fluorine. They are made as volatile derivatives of methane, ethane and propane. The most common CFC is dichlorodifluoromethane, or R-12. Often called Freon, it is used as a refrigerant.

paragraphs.heading: Handy properties
paragraphs.text: CFCs evaporate easily, though less readily than the simple alkanes they come from. Their halogen atoms make the molecules polar, which makes them attract one another more. That polarity makes CFCs useful solvents, and their boiling points suit them to work as refrigerants. They are also far less flammable than methane, and their low toxicity, reactivity and flammability are why they are used so widely.

paragraphs.heading: Used everywhere
paragraphs.text: Many CFCs have served as refrigerants, aerosol propellants, gases for fire suppression systems and solvents. Others work as blowing agents, propellants in medicinal aerosols and degreasing solvents. Nearly every combination of fluorine, chlorine and hydrogen built on methane and ethane has been studied, and most have been sold commercially. Billions of kilograms of chlorodifluoromethane are made each year as a starting material for tetrafluoroethylene, the building block that is turned into Teflon.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the code
paragraphs.text: CFCs carry code numbers such as CFC-12, and there is a quick way to decode them: add 90. The three digits of the result give the number of carbon atoms, then hydrogen atoms, then fluorine atoms. Any carbon bonds left over are filled by chlorine. For CFC-12, 90+12=102, meaning 1 carbon, 0 hydrogens and 2 fluorines, so 2 chlorines are left, giving CCl₂F₂.

paragraphs.heading: Harm to the ozone layer
paragraphs.text: High in the atmosphere, a single chlorine atom, written Cl^(•), lasts a long time and drives the conversion of ozone into O₂. Ozone absorbs UV-B radiation, so losing it lets more of this high-energy radiation reach the ground. Bromine atoms do this even more efficiently, so brominated CFCs are regulated too. Because of their part in ozone depletion, CFCs were phased out under the Montreal Protocol. Replacements include hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), such as R-134a and R-1234yf.

paragraphs.heading: A powerful greenhouse gas
paragraphs.text: The effects of CFCs go beyond the ozone layer. Their carbon-fluorine and carbon-chlorine bonds absorb infrared light most strongly between 7.8 and 15.3 μm. That range is called the atmospheric window, because the air is fairly transparent there. By blocking heat at those wavelengths from escaping Earth's atmosphere, CFCs and other unreactive fluorine gases create a super greenhouse effect.
